fields.title: An operation's property, not a mechanism
fields.keyTakeaway: Idempotency is achieved either by phrasing the action through its final state or via a key. The former is more reliable because it does not depend on client behavior.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: `GET` can be repeated as many times as you like, `POST` cannot. Why is the difference like this, and what should you do about it?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Retries always happen: the network, an impatient user, automation. The question is not whether they will happen, but what will happen when they do. A product where a retry creates a second order will keep creating second orders regardless of care — simply as a consequence of network properties.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: An operation is [[idempotency|idempotent]] if repeating it does not change the result compared to a single execution. Not "does nothing", but "leaves the system in the same state".
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/rows/1/2: Sets the state: "let it be this". Repeating sets the same state
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/rows/2/2: A second deletion changes nothing: the object is already gone
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/rows/3/2: Creates a new one. A repeat creates a second one
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/rows/4/2: "Set status to X" — yes. "Increment by 1" — no
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: The last row shows the core point: **it is not about the method, it is about how the action is phrased.** "Set quantity to 3" is idempotent, "add one" is not. Where there is a choice, phrasing in terms of the final state is safer.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: For operations that must create something new, an [[idempotency-key|idempotency key]] is used. The client generates a token, the server remembers the key-result pair. If a key arrives that has already been seen, we return the saved result without running the operation.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Three product decisions around this mechanism:
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: *When the key is generated.* When the screen opens, not when the button is clicked. Otherwise a second click will produce a new key, and there will be no protection.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: *[[key-retention-window|How long the server remembers the key]].* Usually 24 hours. Too short a window misses delayed retries, too long stores excess data.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: *What counts as the same operation.* The same key with a different request body is a client error, and the server should respond with a conflict rather than executing it.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Inventory of operations for idempotency after a duplicate payment incident.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Already idempotent:* changing an order address (`PUT`), canceling an order (transitioning to a terminal state), marking a notification as read.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Made idempotent via key:* order creation, card charging, bonus accrual.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Rephrased:* bonus accrual used to be "add N points", it became "record accrual for order X in the amount of N". A second call with the same order adds nothing. This proved more reliable than a key because it does not depend on whether the client stored the token.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: *Consciously non-idempotent:* sending a message to support chat. A retry creates a second message, and that is correct — a person might want to write twice.
fields.sections/3/blocks/5/text: Rephrasing through a natural identifier turned out to be the cheapest trick: if an operation has an associated entity, tying it to that entity grants idempotency for free.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Idempotency on our side does not save us if the external provider is not idempotent. Before retrying an external call, you need to know if they support a key; if not, do not retry, only check the status.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Idempotency is achieved either by phrasing the action through the final state or via a key, and the former is more reliable because it does not depend on client behavior.
